Bharaṇī
(‘that which bears’)
------------------------------------------
Bharaṇī is the second of the 27 nakṣatras depicted in the Hindu चलेन्दर्. It is sometimes called as “Apabharaṇī” also. स्तर्स् 35, 39 and 41 in the Meṣa or Aries group comprise this नक्षत्र. In the astrological treatises, its effect is considered as malefic.
See also NAKṢATRA.

Bharata
------------------------------------------
Of the several Bharatas known to the Hindu mythological lore, first comes the emperor भरत, the son of ऋषभ and Jayantī. The country that he ruled came to be known as ‘Ajanābhavarṣa’ or ‘Bharatavarṣa’ or ‘Bhāratavarṣa’.
The son of the king दुष्यन्त and his queen शकुन्तला was also known as भरत; and sometimes, as Sarvadamana.
The Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas were his descendants. Some scholars opine that this country got its name ‘Bharatavarṣa’ from him.
Of all the Bharatas known to the Hindus, भरत of the रामायण, the younger brother of राम, is the most popular. The second son of दशरथ born in the womb of कैकेयी he was deeply devoted to राम. When कैकेयी forced दशरथ, on the pretext of unfulfilled boons given earlier, to banish राम for 14 years and got the kingdom for भरत, he refused to accept it. After chastising his मोथेर्, he went to the चित्रकूट mountain where राम had just settled down, to persuade him to return. Since राम was firm, that obeying the commands of their ड़थेर् दशरथ was binding upon both of them, and advised भरत to rule the kingdom during the period of his banishment, भरत returned to अयोध्या with a heavy heart. He established the pādukās or wooden sandals of राम on the throne at अयोध्या and ruled the kingdom on his behalf from Nandigrāma, a nearby village. He lived like an ascetic till राम returned and then handed back the kingdom to him. During his rule he had considerably improved it. (See also RĀMĀYAṆA.)
Bharata has remained as the model of brotherly love, affection and loyalty for the Hindus over the centuries.
Nāṭyaśāstra, an original treatise on dramaturgy, is ascribed to one भरत who is almost a legendary figure for us now. He might have lived during the period 200 B.C.—A.
. His work as extant today does not seem to be the original. According to अभिनवगुप्त (A.

) the most authoritative commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra of भरत, this work was in 36 chapters comprising 6000 ślokas or verses (vide Abhinava-bhāratī). (See ALAṄKĀRA-ŚASTRA for details.)
The Ṛgveda (3rd and 4th maṇḍalas) mentions Bharatas as a clan of people.

Bhāratī
(‘one who delights in light or knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda (1.142.9) mentions भारती as one of the three goddesses (the other two being Iḷā and सरस्वती) who are requested to reside in the बर्हिस् or sacrificial grass.
In the later literature, भारती has been identified with सरस्वती, the goddess of learning. (See SARASVATĪ for details.)
According to some religious texts, भारती is one of the two consorts of गणपति, the other being Śrī.
‘Bhāratī’ is also one of the ten titles assigned to the मोन्क्स् of the Daśanāmī Order created by शङ्कर (A.

Bhartṛprapañca
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta system is the most well-known of the six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्. It is commanding great respect among the intellectuals even now. शङ्कर (A.
-820), Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) and Madhva (A.

-1276) were the pioneers in the three schools of Vedānta, viz., advaita, viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत, which are popular even today. However, there are other—though less-known—schools of Vedānta, the propagators of some of which preceded even शङ्कर. भर्तृप्रपञ्च was one such. Practically nothing is known of him except that he taught ‘bhedābheda-वाद,’ the doctrine of ‘identity in difference’.
This doctrine is a kind of monism in which both bheda or difference and abheda or identity are accepted between ब्रह्मन् on the one hand and the jīvas, as also the world, on the other. The waves and the foam or the bubbles that arise in the ocean are all identical as water, but different as waves or bubbles. Similarly, the jīvas or the individual souls and the world, which evolve out of ब्रह्मन् are both different and non-different from it.
Bhartṛprapañca accepts pramāṇa-samuccaya, a combination of all the three well-known means of knowledge—pratyakṣa or direct perception, अनुमान or inference and āgama or the वेदस्. As a consequence, he accepts the reality of the world experienced through the sense-organs and hence the need for कर्म or action including ritualistic actions. This leads us to his next proposition of ज्ञान-कर्म-samuccaya, a combination of know-ledge and action, as a means to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. कर्म or desireless action leads to अपवर्ग or freedom from सṁसार (transmigration) and ज्ञान leads to the destruction of अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे, ultimately resulting in identity with ब्रह्मन्, the ultimate Truth.

Bhāratavarṣa
(‘the continent ruled by भरत’)
------------------------------------------
Ancient and medieval Hindu scriptures often refer to India as ‘Bhāratavarṣa,’ ‘Bharatakhaṇḍa,’ ‘Jambū-द्वीप’ and so on. Generally, the country to the south of the हिमालयस् and to the north of the Indian ocean is described as ‘Bhāratavarṣa,’ practically the same as modern India or undivided India.
Sometimes, जम्बूद्वीप is described as comprising nine countries, out of which भारतवर्ष is one. The name ‘Bhārata-varṣa’ might have been derived from the names of its rulers like मनु (who was also called भरत) or भरत, the son of Ṛṣabhadeva or भरत-Sarvadamana, the son of दुष्यन्त and शकुन्तला.
Well-known mountains like Himavat, महेन्द्र and Malaya, and rivers like सरस्वती, गङ्गा, यमुना and गोमती belong to this भारतवर्ष.
Even in the early works it has been admitted that धर्म was fully developed in the भारतवर्ष and that the people were highly cultured.

Bharat Sevashram Sangha
------------------------------------------
This is an organisation of Hindu मोन्क्स् established with the twin ideals of empowering the Hindu society and conduct social service activities. It was established by Svāmī Praṇavānanda (A.

-1941) in 1927.
He was born in Bajitpur (now in Bangladesh) in 1896. As a young man he was extraordinarily strong. A strict vegetarian, he cultivated the habit of meditation right from an early age. At the age of 17, he became a disciple of Bābā Gambhīr-nāthjī and practised severe austerities for five years. He received सṁन्यास at the age of 28 from Svāmī गोविन्दानन्द Giri. He gradually evolved a monastic training programme to be spread over 12 to 14 years.
After setting up a few mobile preaching units in 1924, he officially formed the Bharat Sevashram Sangha—BSS for short—in 1927 with his saṁnyāsin disciples as the trustees led by him. Moral and spiritual regeneration of the Hindu society with special emphasis on physical एदुचतिओन् was an important aspect of its work.
Famine relief work, disaster relief, eradication of untouchability, uniting the depressed classes of the Hindu society and bringing them into the main stream are some of the other programmes of work undertaken by the organisation. Interdining is one of the methods adopted, especially in the rural areas.
Organising Village Defence Units of young men to protect the Hindus during communal riots is also an important contribution of this organisation.
Apart from enlisting eligible persons for सṁन्यास, a system of spiritual initiation for householder devotees has also been evolved. This is normally done by senior मोन्क्स् duly authorised by the organisation.
The founder started in 1935, Hindu Milan Mandirs which act as religious meeting places for all Hindus, without any distinction of caste or creed. For all practical purposes they can be considered as the branches of the organisation.
Serious efforts have also been made to reconvert the Hindus who have left their मोथेर् religion, with appropriate religious ceremonies.
At present, the organisation has 500 मोन्क्स्, 100 āśramas, 450 Milan Mandirs and a large number of service activities. It has also many branches in foreign countries.

Bhārata-sāvitrī
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata is one of the two epics of हिन्दुइस्म्. It has been acclaimed as a veritable encyclopaedia of धर्म or righteousness.
Almost at the very end of this great epic, व्यास, its celebrated author, declares in great anguish that though धर्म is the basis of all wealth and pleasures of life, though he is crying hoarse with both his hands uplifted, none seems to be interested in following it in life! He exhorts people not to abandon धर्म even at the cost of one’s life, let alone out of lust or fear or greed.
The three verses containing his final message (vide Svargārohaṇa-parva, 5.62-64) are called ‘Bhārata-सावित्री’.

Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan
------------------------------------------
Dedicated to spreading Hindu edu-cational and cultural values, the भरतिय विद्य भवन् was founded in A.
(at Bombay, now Mumbai) by K. M. Munshi (A.

-1971), one of the prominent leaders of the freedom movement in India.
Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan at MumbaiTrue to its goal of revitalizing धर्म or the Moral Law, in its threefold form of Satyam (Truth), Śivam (Auspiciousness) and Sundaram (Beauty), the organisation is striving to carry forward India’s ageless message of श्रद्धा (Faith), सṁयम (Self-discipline) and Samarpaṇa (Dedication).
The activities of this Institution are spread over various fields such as एदुचतिओन्, literature, मोरलित्य्, art and culture as also spiritual values.
It has scrupulously kept itself away from the political field.
Over the last seven decades it has established 121 centres all over India and abroad, with 315 constituent institutions. So far it has published 1700 titles of books with sales crossing 26 millions.
Its most valuable publication has been the book, The History and Culture of the Indian People, in eleven volumes.
Through its various institutions it is imparting एदुचतिओन् in subjects like Sanskrit, Indology, Indian Culture including मुसिच्, dance and painting, as also योग, ancient scriptures and languages.
It is also promoting national integration, communal harmony, purity in public life and rural upliftment through suitable programmes.

Bhartṛhari
------------------------------------------
Bhartṛhari is a well-known name in the classical Sanskrit literature. However, we come across two of them.
The first was a grammarian who lived probably in the 5th century A. D. He has been classed among the famous trinity of grammarians—the other two being पाणिनि (400 B. C.) and Nāgeśa or नागोजि भट्ट (18th cent. A. D.)—who developed the स्फोटवाद, the theory that the meaning of a word or a sentence reveals itself in a flash as soon as its utterance is completed. (See SPHOṬAVĀDA.) He is said to have been a Buddhist. Mahābhāṣya-dīpikā and Vākyapadīya are the two works attributed to him. The former is a commentary on the Mahābhāṣya of पतञ्जलि on the sūtras of पाणिनि. The latter is a grammatico-philosophical work in three kāṇḍas or sections dealing with ब्रह्मन्, the Supreme, as शब्द or Logos.
The second भर्तृहरि, whose period has been placed somewhere between 100 B. C. and A.

, was the author of the three well-known Śatakas (one hundred verses) viz., the Śṛṅgāraśataka, the Nīti-śataka and the Vairāgyaśataka. The first deals with erotics, the second with general एथिच्स् and the last with renunciation.
Though very little is known of him, tradition describes him as a king ruling in उज्जयिनी who later abdicated his throne in favour of his younger brother Vikramā-ditya, the originator of the Saṁvat era, since he was disgusted with the infidelity of his queen.

Bharadvāja
------------------------------------------
Bharadvāja (also Bhāradvāja) is the name of a sage that occurs often in the Hindu scriptures. The several Bharadvājas we come across there are obviously different persons. There is one भरद्वाज-Bārhaspatya who is the seer of several hymns of the Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 6). He is probably the same as भरद्वाज, son of बृहस्पति and the ड़थेर् of the well-known द्रोणाचार्य of the Mahābhārata.
The Rāmāyaṇa mentions one Bhara-dvāja, a disciple of वाल्मीकि, who lived in प्रयाग (Allahabad). It was at his instance that राम chose to stay at चित्रकूट. While returning from लङ्का, राम stayed back at his hermitage and sent the information of his coming, through हनुमान्, to भरत.
Bharadvāja is sometimes counted among the seven sages known as ‘gotra-pravartakas’ or the originators of the गोत्र (lineage). His descendants thus became Bhāradvājas.
Two works attributed to a भरद्वाज are available now: Bharadvāja Śrauta-sūtras and Bharadvāja Gṛhyasūtras. The extant manuscript of the former consists of nine praśnas (sections) and part of the tenth. Passages from the latter have been quoted by other dharmaśāstra writers.
The Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य cites the views of a भरद्वाज seven times and of Kaṇiṅka भरद्वाज once. Not much is known of them or their works now.

Bhārgava
(‘a descendant of भृगु’)
------------------------------------------
Though all the descendants of the sage भृगु are entitled to have this patronymic, it is to परशुराम (Rāma of the battle-axe) that this name is particularly applied.
See BHṚGU and PARAŚURĀMA.
